page-029-L:51:γενή.why: The ink has an OMICRON, not an epsilon: a closed round bowl, unlike the open ε of λευκὸν four words later on the same line. γονή (generation, seed) is also what the sentence needs — ὀρνίθων γονή, τὸ μὲν πρῶτον μικρὸν ϗ̀ λευκὸν φαίνεται. Both readers misread the letter; this is the only site in the mark queue where the disagreement was never about a mark at all. ⚠ RESIDUAL RISK, flagged by adversarial review (Grok, 2026-08-08): this is the only change here that alters a BASE LETTER, and base-letter overrides are the class that produced the 40 reverts of 2026-08-08. Sense prefers γονή but cannot by itself separate class (b) — our readers misread — from class (a), Bonitz printed γενή and we should preserve it. Only the ink separates them, and the ink is why this was applied: at 10× the bowl is closed and round, identical to the ο of ὀρνίθων and of τὸ on the same line, and unlike the open mid-stroked ε of μὲν three words on. Worth John's own eye all the same.

page-039-L:1:ταυτὰ.why: A clear raised comma stands over the υ. That is the crasis of τὰ αὐτά, keeping the smooth breathing of the second word, with the grave §154a requires before λεγόμενα. THE MARK ON THIS PAGE IS THE WHOLE ARGUMENT. ⚠ Adversarial review (Grok, 2026-08-08) was right to object to the reasoning I first gave: I pointed at 031-L:49 and 046-R:30, where Bonitz sets ταυτόν and ταυτό bare, and called the mark here "deliberate, not house style". That is backwards. Two absences say the house was not strict; they cannot make a third site's mark intentional, and if anything they should have raised my doubt that the stroke is a fleck. Mixed practice in a 19th-century index is ordinary. The contrast is context; it is not evidence.
